feature: Timeline tracks reorder by dragging their headers
summary: You can now reorder timeline tracks. Press a track's header and drag up or down: the whole track lifts, the other tracks slide aside, and it drops into the gap. The layers list follows the new order.
setup: Photonz Dev, release Next, no switch changed from its default. Open a recording, add a title over it and some music (Sound > Add Sample) so there are four tracks.

try.do: Look at the timeline: Title, V1, Audio, Audio 2, top down.
try.shotNote: Photographed while the Mac was locked. The window is the real one, drawn and driven normally, with one known cost: colours can read dimmed.

try.do: Press V1's header and drag up past the middle of Title. Keep holding.

try.do: Start dragging Title, then press Escape before letting go. It goes back.
Press Cmd-Z. The last move is undone in one step.

evaluate: Does the lifted track look clearly picked up off the timeline, or is the plate and edge too faint on the dark timeline?
Does the swap happen where your hand expects it, as you cross the middle of the next track?
When you drag a track in or out of a group, is it clear from the gap's indent which side you will land on?
Should a group's heading be draggable too, so the whole group moves at once?
rough: No mock draws track reordering. You asked for the layers list's lift on the timeline, so this was checked against that drag rather than a mock frame. The layers list and the tracks now share one model for the gap, the halves and the moved-aside rows.
Only tracks lift. A group's heading does not, so to move a group you move its tracks one at a time.
A locked track does not lift at all, the same as a locked layer. The press just does nothing; nothing on screen explains why.
Premiere does not let you drag tracks, so there is no grown-up habit to match here. The closest one is the layers list in Photoshop, and this works the same way.
The pointer-driven walk needs the Mac to itself and was forced under the lock to get its pictures. Its drag landed correctly.
